title: 7 Delivery Fixes for Experts Who Have the Answer and Sound Unsure Saying It
author: Is Public Speaking
summary: A public-speaking coach argues that many subject-matter experts sound uncertain not because their analysis is weak but because of three fixable mechanical habits: speaking too fast, ending statements with a rising, question-like pitch, and running out of breath mid-sentence. Fast delivery denies listeners the pauses they need to convert words into a decision; rising intonation makes a stated recommendation sound like an open proposal, which happens most often on the very sentences the speaker is least confident they're allowed to assert; and speaking on a nearly-exhausted breath thins the voice and runs sentences together. The piece's core exercise is free and immediate: record yourself delivering a real recommendation for ninety seconds, then count how many sentences end upward, how many filler sounds appear, and how many unnecessary qualifiers you add. The framing throughout is explicitly career-focused: technical thoroughness gets you more analysis requests, but vocal credibility is what gets discussed in promotion conversations.
points: Three specific mechanical habits -- speaking too fast, ending statements with a rising question pitch, and running out of breath mid-sentence -- are what make a correct answer sound uncertain, independent of its content.
Rising intonation on a recommendation gets treated by listeners as an invitation to debate it, and speakers do this most on exactly the sentences they're least sure they're allowed to assert.
The diagnostic is a free, ninety-second phone recording of yourself giving a real recommendation out loud, then counting upward endings, filler sounds, and unnecessary qualifiers.
The author reframes the professional cost in career terms: thorough describes work, but credible describes judgment, and credible is the word that shows up in promotion conversations.
quotes: Your voice came out thinner than you expected, the last three words tilted upward the way they do when you are being careful, and you added a qualifier nobody asked for. Somebody restated your point forty seconds later in a flatter voice, and the room moved with them.

Thorough describes work. Credible describes judgment, and credible is the word that appears in promotion conversations. The colleague with the lower voice and the longer pauses collects it while you collect the analysis requests.
Fast delivery removes the gaps a listener needs to convert your words into a decision, so they stay in listening mode and never reach deciding mode.

Statements delivered with a question's melody get treated as proposals open for debate, and you do it most on the sentences you are least sure you are allowed to say. Those are usually your recommendations.
When you speak on the tail end of an old breath, your voice thins and your sentences run together because you are racing the air you have left.
I found eleven upward endings in ninety seconds the first time I did this, and I had considered myself a decent speaker.
